claim: ieCtnnb1 is located 29,068 base pairs upstream of the transcription starting site for Ctnnb1.
source: a region that is 29,068 base pair (bp) upstream of the transcription starting site for Ctnnb1 displayed typical enhancer feature in intestinal tissues
evidence: The manuscript directly states the genomic location of ieCtnnb1 relative to Ctnnb1.

claim: ieCtnnb1 is enriched with H3K27ac and H3K4me1 in 8-week-old mouse small intestine tissue.
source: The region, named as ieCtnnb1 (intestinal enhancer of Ctnnb1), is at open chromatin status (DNase I hypersensitive site) and enriched with H3K27ac and H3K4me1, two histone marks for active enhancers, in 8-week-old mouse small intestine tissue (Figure 1A).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from ENCODE database showing enrichment of histone marks at ieCtnnb1 in small intestine tissue.

claim: The primary sequence of ieCtnnb1 is not conserved among vertebrates.
source: Notably, unlike neCtnnb1, the primary sequence of ieCtnnb1 is not conserved among vertebrates (Figure 1A, bottom).
evidence: Sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 1A demonstrates lack of conservation.

claim: ieCtnnb1 drives reporter gene expression predominantly at the base of small intestinal crypts and throughout the epithelia of large intestine.
source: Whole-mount β-galactosidase (β-gal) staining of 8-week-old tissues revealed prominent ieCtnnb1-LacZ signals along the GI tract. The signal exhibited a proximal-low to distal-high gradient, with the ileum, cecum, and colon showing the strongest signals (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Reporter mouse experiments with X-gal staining showing spatial expression pattern.

claim: ieCtnnb1 is active in both crypt base columnar cells and Paneth cells.
source: Next, sections of H11i.enh crypts were subjected with β-gal staining followed by immunohistochemistry of OLFM4 (a CBC marker) or lysozyme (a PC marker). Data showed X-gal signals are in close proximity with both OLFM4 and lysozyme (Figure 1C), suggesting that the activity of ieCtnnb1 is present in both CBCs and PCs.
evidence: Co-staining experiments showing overlap of reporter activity with cell type markers.

claim: Knockout of ieCtnnb1 led to a 26.5% reduction in Ctnnb1 expression in small intestinal crypts.
source: We then collected crypts from small and large intestine, finding that the expression levels of Ctnnb1 were decreased by 26.5% and 22.3% respectively in Ctnnb1Δi.enh crypts (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: RT-qPCR measurements comparing Ctnnb1 expression levels between wild-type and knockout mice.

claim: Knockout of ieCtnnb1 led to a 22.3% reduction in Ctnnb1 expression in large intestinal crypts.
source: We then collected crypts from small and large intestine, finding that the expression levels of Ctnnb1 were decreased by 26.5% and 22.3% respectively in Ctnnb1Δi.enh crypts (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: RT-qPCR measurements comparing Ctnnb1 expression levels between wild-type and knockout mice.

claim: The expression level of Ctnnb1 in the Ctnnb1Δi.enh liver remained unaltered.
source: In contrast, the expression level of Ctnnb1 in the Ctnnb1Δi.enh liver remained unaltered (Figure 1—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: RT-qPCR measurements showing no change in Ctnnb1 expression in liver tissue.

claim: Nuclear β-catenin levels decreased by 49.5% in small intestinal crypts of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice.
source: We therefore carried out nuclear/cytosol fractionation assays, which revealed a substantial decrease in the levels of both nuclear (49.5%) and cytosolic (29.8%) β-catenin in small intestinal crypts of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: Nuclear/cytosol fractionation followed by immunoblotting quantification.

claim: Cytosolic β-catenin levels decreased by 29.8% in small intestinal crypts of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice.
source: We therefore carried out nuclear/cytosol fractionation assays, which revealed a substantial decrease in the levels of both nuclear (49.5%) and cytosolic (29.8%) β-catenin in small intestinal crypts of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: Nuclear/cytosol fractionation followed by immunoblotting quantification.

claim: Loss of ieCtnnb1 compromised the canonical Wnt signaling in intestinal crypts.
source: Together, the loss of ieCtnnb1 compromised the Wnt signaling in intestinal epithelia by reducing Ctnnb1 transcription.
evidence: RNA-seq and RT-qPCR showing reduced expression of Wnt target genes in knockout mice.

claim: The proportion of Paneth cells was decreased by 49.2% in Ctnnb1Δi.enh crypts.
source: Second, the proportion of PCs was decreased by 49.2% in Ctnnb1Δi.enh crypts, which was confirmed by the immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of Defensin 5α, a PC marker (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Single-cell sequencing data and IHC quantification showing reduced Paneth cell numbers.

claim: The number of Ki67-positive cells was decreased by 16.1% in Ctnnb1Δi.enh small intestinal epithelia.
source: Consistently, the numbers of Ki67-positive cells and EdU-labeled cells (4 hr pulse) were decreased by 16.1% and 21.9%, respectively, in Ctnnb1Δi.enh small intestinal epithelia (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: IHC quantification of Ki67-positive proliferating cells.

claim: The number of EdU-labeled cells was decreased by 21.9% in Ctnnb1Δi.enh small intestinal epithelia.
source: Consistently, the numbers of Ki67-positive cells and EdU-labeled cells (4 hr pulse) were decreased by 16.1% and 21.9%, respectively, in Ctnnb1Δi.enh small intestinal epithelia (Figure 2K and L).
evidence: EdU pulse-labeling experiment quantification.

claim: The survival period of Ctnnb1Δi.enh;ApcMin/+ mice (median survival – 255 days) was significantly longer than the ApcMin/+ mice (median survival – 165 days).
source: The survival period of Ctnnb1Δi.enh;ApcMin/+ mice (median survival – 255 days) was significantly longer than the ApcMin/+ mice (median survival – 165 days), with the former having a heavier body weight (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: Survival analysis comparing two mouse genotypes.

claim: Ctnnb1Δi.enh;ApcMin/+ mice barely grow colorectal cancers and have much fewer intestinal tumors compared to ApcMin/+ mice.
source: Strikingly, the Ctnnb1Δi.enh;ApcMin/+ mice barely grow CRCs and have much fewer intestinal tumors compared to ApcMin/+ mice, with significantly smaller tumor area (Figure 3B and D–F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Tumor counting and area measurements in mouse models.

claim: Ablation of ieCtnnb1 deters tumorigenesis of intestinal cancers by suppressing the Wnt signaling.
source: Thus, ablation of ieCtnnb1 deters tumorigenesis of intestinal cancers by suppressing the Wnt signaling.
evidence: Multiple lines of evidence including tumor burden, proliferation markers, and gene expression in ApcMin/+ mice.

claim: Human ieCTNNB1 is located 38,489 bp upstream of human CTNNB1.
source: A region with open chromatin (DNase I hypersensitivity) and enrichment of H3K27ac/H3K4me1 was identified at 38,489 bp upstream of human CTNNB1 in adult small intestine and colon tissues (Figure 4A).
evidence: ENCODE data showing genomic location of human enhancer.

claim: ieCTNNB1 could drive LacZ expression in the bottom of small intestinal crypts and the entire epithelia of large intestine.
source: We generated ieCTNNB1 reporter mice (H11hi.enh) and observed that ieCTNNB1 could drive LacZ expression in the bottom of small intestinal crypts and the entire epithelia of large intestine, also exhibiting a proximal-low to distal-high pattern (Figure 4B).
evidence: Reporter mouse experiments with X-gal staining showing spatial expression pattern.

claim: CRISPR-mediated activation of ieCTNNB1 enhanced transcription of CTNNB1 in HCT-15 cells.
source: We then conducted CRISPR-mediated activation and interference in HCT-15 CRC cells using three guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting ieCTNNB1, which respectively enhanced and inhibited transcription of CTNNB1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: CRISPRa experiments showing increased CTNNB1 expression.

claim: CRISPR-mediated interference of ieCTNNB1 inhibited transcription of CTNNB1 in HCT-15 cells.
source: We then conducted CRISPR-mediated activation and interference in HCT-15 CRC cells using three guide RNAs (gRNAs) targeting ieCTNNB1, which respectively enhanced and inhibited transcription of CTNNB1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: CRISPRi experiments showing decreased CTNNB1 expression.

claim: The enrichment of H3K27ac at ieCTNNB1 in CRC tissues were significantly higher than that in native tissues.
source: Essentially, the enrichment of H3K27ac at ieCTNNB1 in CRC tissues were significantly higher than that in native tissues (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from 64 paired CRC and adjacent normal tissue samples.

claim: The enrichment of H3K27ac at ieCTNNB1 positively correlated with the expression of CTNNB1.
source: Moreover, the enrichment of H3K27ac at ieCTNNB1 positively correlated with the expression of CTNNB1, but the enrichment of H3K4me3 at CTNNB1's promoter was not associated with CTNNB1's expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: Correlation analysis between ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data from CRC samples.

claim: The enrichment of H3K4me3 at CTNNB1's promoter was not associated with CTNNB1's expression.
source: Moreover, the enrichment of H3K27ac at ieCTNNB1 positively correlated with the expression of CTNNB1, but the enrichment of H3K4me3 at CTNNB1's promoter was not associated with CTNNB1's expression (Figure 5D).
evidence: Correlation analysis between ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data from CRC samples.

claim: The SNP rs15981379 (C>T) within ieCTNNB1 is inversely correlated with the expression levels of CTNNB1 in the esophagus and transverse colon.
source: Importantly, the C>T variation is inversely correlated with the expression levels of CTNNB1 in the esophagus and transverse colon (Figure 5E).
evidence: eQTL analysis from GTEx database showing association between SNP and gene expression.

claim: The C>T variation at rs15981379 compromised luciferase activity driven by the ieCTNNB1 region 1.
source: Luciferase reporter assays in HCT116 and HeLa cells revealed that the C>T variation indeed compromised luciferase activity driven by the ieCTNNB1 region 1 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assays comparing wild-type and variant sequences.

claim: Decreasing the expression of CREB1 could compromise CTNNB1's transcription in HCT-15 cells.
source: We then transduced shRNAs-expressing plasmids into HCT-15 cells to individually downregulate their expressions, revealing that decreasing the expression of CREB1 (cAMP responsive element binding protein 1) or HNF4A (hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 alpha) could compromise CTNNB1's transcription (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: shRNA knockdown experiments followed by RT-qPCR measurements.

claim: Decreasing the expression of HNF4A could compromise CTNNB1's transcription in HCT-15 cells.
source: We then transduced shRNAs-expressing plasmids into HCT-15 cells to individually downregulate their expressions, revealing that decreasing the expression of CREB1 (cAMP responsive element binding protein 1) or HNF4A (hepatocyte nuclear factor 4 alpha) could compromise CTNNB1's transcription (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: shRNA knockdown experiments followed by RT-qPCR measurements.

claim: Enrichment of p-S133-CREB1 was more prominent than CREB1 at ieCtnnb1 in small intestinal crypts.
source: ChIP-qPCR experiments showed that enrichment of p-S133-CREB1 was more prominent than CREB1 at ieCtnnb1 in small intestinal crypts and at ieCTNNB1 in HCT-15 cells (Figure 6C and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR experiments comparing enrichment of phosphorylated and total CREB1.

claim: Enrichment of p-S133-CREB1 was more prominent than CREB1 at ieCTNNB1 in HCT-15 cells.
source: ChIP-qPCR experiments showed that enrichment of p-S133-CREB1 was more prominent than CREB1 at ieCtnnb1 in small intestinal crypts and at ieCTNNB1 in HCT-15 cells (Figure 6C and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR experiments comparing enrichment of phosphorylated and total CREB1.

claim: HNF4α and p-S133-CREB1 bind to multiple subregions of ieCTNNB1 and ieCtnnb1, as well as the promoters of CTNNB1 and Ctnnb1.
source: Notably, HNF4α and p-S133-CREB1 bind to multiple subregions of ieCTNNB1 and ieCtnnb1, as well as the promoters of CTNNB1 and Ctnnb1 (pCTNNB1 and pCtnnb1) in HCT-15 cells and small intestinal crypts (Figure 6C and D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR experiments showing binding at multiple genomic regions.

claim: Expression levels of CREB1 were significantly higher in colon and rectum cancer samples than those of normal tissues.
source: By analyzing the GEIPA-COAD (colon adenocarcinoma) and READ (rectum adenocarcinoma) database, expression levels of CREB1 and HNF4A were found to be significantly higher in colon and rectum cancer samples than those of normal tissues (Figure 6E).
evidence: Analysis of GEPIA database comparing gene expression in tumor vs normal tissues.

claim: Expression levels of HNF4A were significantly higher in colon and rectum cancer samples than those of normal tissues.
source: By analyzing the GEIPA-COAD (colon adenocarcinoma) and READ (rectum adenocarcinoma) database, expression levels of CREB1 and HNF4A were found to be significantly higher in colon and rectum cancer samples than those of normal tissues (Figure 6E).
evidence: Analysis of GEPIA database comparing gene expression in tumor vs normal tissues.

claim: Expression levels of CREB1 positively correlated with that of CTNNB1 in colon and rectum cancers.
source: Furthermore, expression levels of CREB1 and HNF4A positively correlated with that of CTNNB1 (Figure 6F).
evidence: Correlation analysis of gene expression data from GEPIA database.

claim: Expression levels of HNF4A positively correlated with that of CTNNB1 in colon and rectum cancers.
source: Furthermore, expression levels of CREB1 and HNF4A positively correlated with that of CTNNB1 (Figure 6F).
evidence: Correlation analysis of gene expression data from GEPIA database.

claim: HNF4α was significantly enriched at the promoter of Ctnnb1 in Apc mutation induced colon cancer tissues.
source: HNF4α and p-S133-CREB1 were significantly enriched at the promoter of Ctnnb1 in Apc mutation induced colon cancer tissues (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR experiments in ApcMin/+ mouse tumor tissues.

claim: p-S133-CREB1 was significantly enriched at the promoter of Ctnnb1 in Apc mutation induced colon cancer tissues.
source: HNF4α and p-S133-CREB1 were significantly enriched at the promoter of Ctnnb1 in Apc mutation induced colon cancer tissues (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR experiments in ApcMin/+ mouse tumor tissues.

claim: Knockout of ieCtnnb1 greatly diminished the association of HNF4α with Ctnnb1's promoter.
source: Intriguingly, knockout of ieCtnnb1 greatly diminished the association of HNF4α and p-S133-CREB1 with Ctnnb1's promoter (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR experiments comparing wild-type and ieCtnnb1 knockout tumor tissues.

claim: Knockout of ieCtnnb1 greatly diminished the association of p-S133-CREB1 with Ctnnb1's promoter.
source: Intriguingly, knockout of ieCtnnb1 greatly diminished the association of HNF4α and p-S133-CREB1 with Ctnnb1's promoter (Figure 6G and H).
evidence: ChIP-qPCR experiments comparing wild-type and ieCtnnb1 knockout tumor tissues.

claim: The body weight of 8-week-old male Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice was slightly but significantly lighter than that of wild-type controls.
source: Interestingly, the body weight of 8-week-old male Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice was slightly but significantly lighter than that of wild-type controls (Figure 1D and F)
evidence: Body weight measurements comparing knockout and wild-type mice.

claim: The length of small and large intestines of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice was comparable to that of control mice.
source: but the length of small and large intestines of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice was comparable to that of control mice (Figure 1E, G, and H).
evidence: Intestinal length measurements showing no significant difference.

claim: ieCtnnb1 resides in the same topologically associating domain (TAD) with Ctnnb1.
source: Interestingly, we noticed that a region that is 29,068 base pair (bp) upstream of the transcription starting site for Ctnnb1 displayed typical enhancer feature in intestinal tissues and resides in the same topologically associating domain (TAD) with Ctnnb1 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Hi-C data showing TAD boundaries and genomic locations.

claim: ieCTNNB1 resides in the same TAD as the promoter of CTNNB1.
source: Similar to ieCtnnb1, the 3-kb-long human genomic region, named as ieCTNNB1, resides in the same TAD as the promoter of CTNNB1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Hi-C data from SW480 cells showing TAD boundaries.

claim: The 2,153 bp core region of ieCtnnb1 could drive the expression of luciferase reporter in multiple cell types.
source: First, the 2,153 bp core region (CR), representing the H3K27ac peak region of ieCtnnb1, could drive the expression of luciferase reporter in multiple cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assays in HEK293T, HCT116, and HeLa cells.

claim: Each of the five ieCTNNB1 subregions individually increased luciferase activity in both HCT116 and HeLa cells.
source: Experiments demonstrated that each of the five ieCTNNB1 subregions individually increased luciferase activity in both HCT116 and HeLa cells (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Luciferase reporter assays testing different subregions of ieCTNNB1.

claim: The enrichment of H3K27ac at ieCtnnb1 is prominent in embryonic intestine and stomach tissue, as well as in adult kidney and liver.
source: Importantly, the enrichment of H3K27ac at ieCtnnb1 is also prominent in embryonic intestine and stomach tissue, as well as in adult kidney and liver (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and D).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from ENCODE showing H3K27ac enrichment in multiple tissues.

claim: The enrichment of H3K27ac at ieCtnnb1 was not detected in non-GI tissues such as embryonic and adult brain.
source: In contrast, the enrichment was not detected in non-GI tissues such as embryonic and adult brain (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: ChIP-seq data from ENCODE showing absence of H3K27ac enrichment in brain tissues.

claim: The enrichment of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 at ieCtnnb1 is negligible in all examined tissues.
source: In line with signatures of active enhancers, the enrichment of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 at ieCtnnb1 is negligible in all examined tissues (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: ChIP-seq data showing lack of H3K4me3 and H3K36me3 enrichment at ieCtnnb1.

claim: The expression of genes located in the same TAD as Ctnnb1 and ieCtnnb1, including Ulk4, Rpl14, and Entpd3, was not changed in Ctnnb1Δi.enh small intestinal crypts.
source: In addition, the expression of genes located in the same TAD as Ctnnb1 and ieCtnnb1, including Ulk4, Rpl14, and Entpd3, was not changed in Ctnnb1Δi.enh small intestinal crypts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: RT-qPCR measurements showing no change in expression of neighboring genes.

claim: ieCtnnb1 plays a specific role in regulating the transcription of Ctnnb1 in intestinal epithelia.
source: These data suggest that ieCtnnb1 plays a specific role in regulating the transcription of Ctnnb1 in intestinal epithelia.
evidence: Tissue-specific expression changes and lack of effect on neighboring genes.

claim: The canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling is essential for the construction and homeostasis of intestinal epithelia.
source: The canonical Wnt/β-catenin signaling is essential for the construction and homeostasis of intestinal epithelia (Mah et al., 2016).
evidence: Citation to established literature on Wnt signaling in intestinal homeostasis.

claim: Expression levels of markers for secretory cells were greatly reduced in all small intestinal crypt cells of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice.
source: Expression levels of markers for secretory cells were greatly reduced whereas levels of markers for absorptive cells were elevated in all small intestinal crypt cells of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice.
evidence: Single-cell RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression patterns.

claim: Levels of markers for absorptive cells were elevated in all small intestinal crypt cells of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice.
source: Expression levels of markers for secretory cells were greatly reduced whereas levels of markers for absorptive cells were elevated in all small intestinal crypt cells of Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice.
evidence: Single-cell RNA-seq data showing differential gene expression patterns.

claim: The pool size of CBCs was not significantly altered in Ctnnb1Δi.enh mice.
source: Knockout of ieCtnnb1 decreases number of PCs by almost 50% but the pool size of CBCs was not significantly altered.
evidence: Single-cell sequencing data showing cell type proportions.

claim: The enhancer activity of ieCTNNB1 in colorectal cancer tissues was stronger than that in adjacent normal tissues.
source: The enhancer activity of ieCTNNB1 in colorectal cancer tissues was stronger than that in adjacent normal tissues.
evidence: ChIP-seq data showing higher H3K27ac enrichment at ieCTNNB1 in tumor vs normal tissues.

claim: The enhancer activity of ieCTNNB1 in CRC tissues positively correlates with CTNNB1 expression levels.
source: The enhancer activity of ieCTNNB1 in CRC tissues is higher than that in adjacent normal tissues and positively correlates with CTNNB1 expression levels.
evidence: Correlation analysis between H3K27ac ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: HNF4α plays crucial roles in the normal development of the colon and the maintenance of epithelial barrier.
source: Of note, HNF4α plays crucial roles in the normal development of the colon and the maintenance of epithelial barrier (Garrison et al., 2006; Cattin et al., 2009).
evidence: Citations to published studies on HNF4α function.

claim: The phosphorylation of CREB1 at serine 133 (p-S133-CREB1) is essential for its role in activation of gene transcription.
source: The phosphorylation of CREB1 at serine 133 (p-S133-CREB1) is essential for its role in activation of gene transcription (Carlezon et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation to published study on CREB1 phosphorylation and function.

claim: Mouse ieCtnnb1 and human ieCTNNB1 do not share significant homology in primary sequence.
source: Very intriguingly, unlike the highly conserved neCtnnb1 sequence among amniotes, mouse ieCtnnb1 and human ieCTNNB1 do not share significant homology in primary sequence (Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: Sequence comparison analysis and citation to previous work.

claim: Both ieCtnnb1 and ieCTNNB1 localize at the intergenic region 30–40 kb upstream of Ctnnb1's promoter.
source: Nonetheless, both ieCtnnb1 and ieCTNNB1 localize at the intergenic region 30–40 kb upstream of Ctnnb1's promoter.
evidence: Genomic location data from ENCODE and Hi-C analyses.

claim: Both ieCtnnb1 and ieCTNNB1 contain binding motifs for HNF4α and CREB1.
source: Moreover, both ieCtnnb1 and ieCTNNB1 contain binding motifs for HNF4α and CREB1.
evidence: Motif analysis using JASPAR database.

claim: Conserved TF binding motifs stabilize and preserve enhancer functionality over evolution.
source: These findings support the notion that conserved TF binding motifs stabilize and preserve enhancer functionality over evolution (Zabidi and Stark, 2016; Wong et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations to published studies on enhancer evolution.

claim: ieCtnnb1 and ieCTNNB1 contain distinct TF binding motifs, which may respectively exert species-specific roles in regulating the transcription of Ctnnb1/CTNNB1.
source: Of note, ieCtnnb1 and ieCTNNB1 contain distinct TF binding motifs, which may respectively exert species-specific roles in regulating the transcription of Ctnnb1/CTNNB1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Motif analysis showing species-specific binding sites.

claim: The β-catenin-dependent canonical Wnt signaling is pivotal in organ development, tissue homeostasis, and cancer.
source: The β-catenin-dependent canonical Wnt signaling is pivotal in organ development, tissue homeostasis, and cancer.
evidence: General statement supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: ieCTNNB1 contains a single-nucleotide polymorphism associated with CTNNB1 expression levels in human gastrointestinal epithelia.
source: ieCTNNB1 contains a single-nucleotide polymorphism associated with CTNNB1 expression levels in human gastrointestinal epithelia.
evidence: eQTL analysis from GTEx database showing association between SNP and gene expression.

claim: HNF4α and phosphorylated CREB1 were identified as key trans-factors binding to ieCTNNB1 and regulating CTNNB1 transcription.
source: HNF4α and phosphorylated CREB1 were identified as key trans-factors binding to ieCTNNB1 and regulating CTNNB1 transcription.
evidence: ChIP-qPCR and knockdown experiments showing binding and functional effects.

claim: Enterocytes constitute approximately 90% of all differentiated cells in the gastrointestinal epithelium.
source: Enterocytes (ECs) constitute ~90% of all differentiated cells and function as highly efficient cells for absorbing nutrients and water (Snoeck et al., 2005).
evidence: Citation to published study on intestinal cell composition.

claim: Goblet cells produce mucus to lubricate the mucosal surface.
source: Goblet cells (GCs) produce mucus to lubricate the mucosal surface (Gustafsson and Johansson, 2022).
evidence: Citation to published study on goblet cell function.

claim: Enteroendocrine cells sense luminal nutrients and secrete peptide hormones to regulate appetite, intestinal motility, and insulin release.
source: Enteroendocrine cells (EECs) sense luminal nutrients and secrete peptide hormones to regulate appetite, intestinal motility, and insulin release (Gribble and Reimann, 2019).
evidence: Citation to published study on enteroendocrine cell function.

claim: Tuft cells are chemosensory cells that respond to various stimuli including infections and hypoxia.
source: Tuft cells (TCs) are chemosensory cells that respond to various stimuli including infections and hypoxia (Schneider et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to published study on tuft cell function.

claim: Lgr5-expressing crypt base columnar cells are actively dividing stem cells.
source: While the prevailing belief is that Lgr5-expressing crypt base columnar (CBC) cells are actively dividing stem cells and Bmi-expressing '+4' cells (positioned four cells above the base of the crypt) are slowly cycling stem cells, it's important to note that crypt cells have the capacity for fate reprogramming and de-differentiation to sustain regenerative capability (Barker et al., 2007; Tian et al., 2011; Yan et al., 2012; Metcalfe et al., 2014; Beumer and Clevers, 2016).
evidence: Citations to multiple published studies on intestinal stem cells.

claim: Paneth cells secret antimicrobial peptides, called defensins, thereby contributing to host defense against microbes.
source: In addition to stem and progenitor cells, the base of small intestinal crypts contains Paneth cells (PCs) that secret antimicrobial peptides, called defensins, thereby contributing to host defense against microbes (Lueschow and McElroy, 2020; Barreto et al., 2022).
evidence: Citations to published studies on Paneth cell function.

claim: Paneth cells contribute to the stem cell niche function by secreting Wnt ligands to maintain epithelial homeostasis of the small intestine.
source: PCs also contribute to the stem cell niche function, e.g., secreting Wnt ligands, to maintain epithelial homeostasis of the small intestine (Sato et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to published study on Paneth cell niche function.

claim: Inhibition of Wnt ligand secretion reduced the number of functional stem cells and led to a faster crypt fixation rate.
source: Inhibition of Wnt ligand secretion reduced the number of functional stem cells and led to a faster crypt fixation rate (Huels et al., 2018).
evidence: Citation to published study on Wnt signaling and stem cell function.

claim: Reduced Wnt signaling in stem cells and the niche of intestinal crypts during aging causes inhibition of proliferation and reduced numbers of intestinal stem cells.
source: In the process of aging, reduced Wnt signaling in stem cells and the niche of intestinal crypts causes inhibition of proliferation and reduced numbers of intestinal stem cells (Nalapareddy et al., 2017; Pentinmikko et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to published studies on aging and Wnt signaling.

claim: The Wnt signal is essential for commitment, maturation, and location of Paneth cells and other secretory cells.
source: The Wnt signal is also essential for commitment, maturation, and location of PCs and other secretory cells (van Es et al., 2005; Andreu et al., 2008).
evidence: Citations to published studies on Wnt signaling and secretory cell differentiation.

claim: Wnt, EGF, and Delta-like 1/4 ligands presented by Paneth cells sustained CBCs' proliferative states and production.
source: On the other hand, Wnt, EGF, and Delta-like 1/4 ligands presented by PCs sustained CBCs' proliferative states and the production (Sato et al., 2011).
evidence: Citation to published study on niche signals supporting stem cells.

claim: Aberrant activation of canonical Wnt signaling is associated with GI cancers, most notably colorectal cancer.
source: Aberrant activation of canonical Wnt signaling is associated with GI cancers, most notably colorectal cancer (CRC) (Zhao et al., 2022; Zhu and Li, 2023).
evidence: Citations to published studies on Wnt signaling in colorectal cancer.

claim: Germinal mutations of the APC gene underlie the familial adenomatous polyposis, a hereditary neoplastic syndrome and the pre-cancerous condition for CRC.
source: Germinal mutations of the APC gene, which encodes the negative regulator of β-catenin, underlie the familial adenomatous polyposis, a hereditary neoplastic syndrome and the pre-cancerous condition for CRC (Cheng et al., 2019; Li et al., 2021a).
evidence: Citations to published studies on APC mutations and familial adenomatous polyposis.

claim: APC is mutated in up to 80% of human sporadic CRCs.
source: Moreover, APC is mutated in up to 80% of human sporadic CRCs (Li et al., 2021b).
evidence: Citation to published study on APC mutation frequency in CRC.

claim: Inactivation of APC causes enhanced accumulation of β-catenin in nuclei and subsequent activation of proliferative and pro-survival signals in CRC cells.
source: Inactivation of APC causes enhanced accumulation of β-catenin in nuclei and subsequent activation of proliferative and pro-survival signals in CRC cells (Cheng et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to published study on APC function and β-catenin regulation.

claim: The transcriptional activity of CTNNB1 is enhanced in CRCs.
source: Interestingly, the transcriptional activity of CTNNB1, the coding gene for β-catenin, is also enhanced in CRCs (Terrin et al., 2017); however, the underlying mechanism is largely unknown.
evidence: Citation to published study on CTNNB1 transcription in CRC.

claim: Enhancers are essential cis-regulatory DNA elements that control spatiotemporal gene expressions during cell fate specification and maintenance.
source: Enhancers are essential cis-regulatory DNA elements that control spatiotemporal gene expressions during cell fate specification and maintenance (Pachano et al., 2022).
evidence: Citation to published study on enhancer function.

claim: Active enhancers are often associated with cell fate specifiers, mostly transcription factors, and are enriched with specific histone modification such as H3K27ac and H3K4me1.
source: Active enhancers are often associated with cell fate specifiers, mostly transcription factors (TFs), and are enriched with specific histone modification such as H3K27ac (acetylated lysine 27 of histone H3) and H3K4me1 (mono-methylated lysine 4) of histone H3 (Jindal and Farley, 2021).
evidence: Citation to published study on enhancer chromatin marks.

claim: Variations of enhancer sequences often lead to aberrant gene silence and activation, thereby causing developmental anomalies and cancers.
source: Importantly, variations of enhancer sequences often lead to aberrant gene silence and activation, thereby causing developmental anomalies and cancers (Zabidi and Stark, 2016; Sengupta and George, 2017; Kvon et al., 2021).
evidence: Citations to published studies on enhancer variation and disease.

claim: The proper expression of essential fate genes in different cell types is often controlled by specific enhancers.
source: The proper expression of essential fate genes in different cell types is often controlled by specific enhancers (Kvon et al., 2021; Pachano et al., 2022).
evidence: Citations to published studies on cell-type-specific enhancers.

claim: The LacZ signal driven by human ieCTNNB1 was less intense than that driven by mouse ieCtnnb1.
source: Notably, the LacZ signal driven by human ieCTNNB1 was less intense than that driven by mouse ieCtnnb1, potentially attributed to species-specific TF-enhancer interactions.
evidence: Comparison of reporter gene expression in mouse models.

claim: The decreased level of BAMBI resulting from the loss of ieCtnnb1 further reduced nuclear β-catenin.
source: Although the loss of ieCtnnb1 should not directly lead to reduced nuclear translocation of β-catenin, RNA-seq results showed that the loss of ieCtnnb1 causes a reduction in the expression of Bambi (BMP and activin membrane-bound inhibitor), a target gene in the canonical Wnt signaling pathway (Figure 1M). BAMBI promotes the binding of Frizzled to Dishevelled, thereby stabilizing β-catenin and facilitating its nuclear translocation (Lin et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2014; Mai et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015). Thus, it is likely that the decreased level of BAMBI resulting from the loss of ieCtnnb1 further reduced nuclear β-catenin.
evidence: RNA-seq data showing reduced Bambi expression and citations to studies on BAMBI function.

claim: The intestinal specificity of ieCtnnb1 makes it an ideal target to lower the strength of Wnt signaling in treating CRC without affecting other tissues.
source: Therefore, the intestinal specificity of ieCtnnb1 makes it an ideal target to lower the strength of Wnt signaling in treating CRC without affecting other tissues (Hamdan and Johnsen, 2019; Orouji et al., 2022).
evidence: Tissue-specific activity of ieCtnnb1 and citations to studies on Wnt targeting strategies.

claim: Homozygous ieCtnnb1 knockout mice were born in Mendelian ratios and thrived through adulthood.
source: Homozygous ieCtnnb1 knockout (Ctnnb1Δi.enh) mice were born in Mendelian ratios and thrived through adulthood.
evidence: Observation of mouse breeding and survival.

claim: The number of goblet cells was slightly (not statistically significant) reduced upon loss of ieCtnnb1.
source: The number of GCs was slightly (not statistically significant) reduced upon loss of ieCtnnb1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Histological quantification showing trend but no statistical significance.

claim: Genetic removal of Paneth cells leads to the concomitant loss of Lgr5+ stem cells.
source: A previous study showed that genetic removal of PCs leads to the concomitant loss of Lgr5+ stem cells (Sato et al., 2011), while other studies indicated that PCs are not mandatory niche cells for the intestinal epithelia (Garabedian et al., 1997; Durand et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to published studies on Paneth cell function in stem cell maintenance.

claim: Paneth cells are not mandatory niche cells for the intestinal epithelia.
source: A previous study showed that genetic removal of PCs leads to the concomitant loss of Lgr5+ stem cells (Sato et al., 2011), while other studies indicated that PCs are not mandatory niche cells for the intestinal epithelia (Garabedian et al., 1997; Durand et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: Citations to published studies showing conflicting results on Paneth cell necessity.

claim: Essential Wnt ligands are primarily supplied by subepithelial stromal populations.
source: Although Wnt ligands provided by PCs may support Lgr5+ CBCs, essential Wnt ligands are primarily supplied by subepithelial stromal populations (Degirmenci et al., 2018; Shoshkes-Carmel et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations to published studies on sources of Wnt ligands in intestinal niche.

claim: The presence of redundancy at the stem cell niche enhances the accuracy in maintaining intestinal homeostasis.
source: The presence of redundancy at the stem cell niche enhances the accuracy in maintaining intestinal homeostasis.
evidence: Inference from multiple sources of niche signals.

claim: Different truncations or mutations of APC lead to specific tumor types throughout the body in a Wnt/β-catenin dosage-dependent manner.
source: Different truncations or mutations of APC lead to specific tumor types throughout the body in a Wnt/β-catenin dosage-dependent manner. For example, although Apc1638N;Ctnnb1+/-mice were less prone to GI cancers, Apc1638N;Ctnnb1+/- female animals tended to grow breast cancers (Bakker et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to published study on APC mutations and tissue-specific tumorigenesis.
